rv.q: So confident is “Priscilla, Queen of the Desert” in its ability to ramp up the thrills that it doesn’t wait for the finale to drop the confetti — it falls a mere 30 minutes in shamelessly feel-good show won’t do to entertain, from bringing theatergoers onstage to dance to lowering its singing divas from the rafters.
Big, brassy, unapologetically profane and over the top — it's no wonder Bette Midler signed on as a producer.
Inartful here, crass there, this rollicking crowdpleaser in sequins nonetheless packs enough heart to leave the masses enthralled.
There is much to enjoy in this spectacular-looking, stubbornly-sentimental, disco-throbbing jukebox adaptation of the edgier 1994 indie-film hit, especially in the stronger second act.
Some people -- many people, likely -- won't be able to get enough of 'Priscilla,' Others may be put off by its relentless naughtiness
Priscilla Queen of the Desert has colorful artifice to spare—those costumes!—but nearly nothing about it rings true.

The show is simultaneously too much and not enough: too much noise and glitter, not enough heart and specificity.

You might recall that Gardiner wore a self-made dress of Gold American Express cards to the Oscar-cast and her designs for the on-stage Priscilla are just as delightfully eye-catching and colorfully hilarious.
A charming little movie has been made into a hard-sell stage musical overloaded with kitsch--and it's fun!
"Priscilla" will do anything to try to entertain - even stooping to dragging audience members on stage for a dance number - and it succeeds often enough to be appealing.

While the show will likely prove to be a crowd-pleaser, it can be difficult to tell whether all of those offering a standing ovation at the curtain call actually enjoyed what they saw — or are simply surrendering out of sheer exhaustion.
The first tipoff to the desired ambiance at 'Priscilla Queen of the Desert' is severe-faced Broadway ushers sporting huge purple boas.
Call me a party pooper, but that was enough to make this supposed frolic a drag.
You really want to have fun, but it is so aggressively campy that it soon becomes irritating and too much to stomach.
“Priscilla” skimps on sincerity in its musical storytelling to provide instead a somewhat overwhelming cavalcade of madly ga-ga couture and feverish choreography deployed in wacko production numbers.

sg.ra: After the 2023 TSX lift the orchestra received wider seats and a slight rake, and center rows G-K are the unobstructed sweet spot before the mezzanine overhang begins at Row K per the official chart; AVFMS reports suggest the overhang only becomes visually noticeable closer to Row N-O, so center G-K is the cleanest post-reno picture.

sg.vl: Discount seats but mezz starts to bite
sg.ra: The mezzanine overhang begins cutting in roughly at Orchestra Row K per the theatre's official seating chart, so rear-orchestra tickets (Row N onward) are priced well below center-premium but you give up the top of the proscenium; one AVFMS reviewer at Row N seat 119 still reported no overhang intrusion, so the rear orch is a real value play on non-spectacle shows that don't use high flying scenery.

Post-2023 lift reviewers specifically call out that the front-mezz sightline is 'incredible' and gives a panoramic view of the choreography, and multiple sources name center Rows A-C (or middle C-F) as the unobstructed sweet spot; avoid the first two side-aisle seats in Row A which Broadway Direct flags as obstructed by a safety railing that survived the renovation.

Unlike most Broadway houses, the Palace rear mezz sits on the same elevated tier rather than under a balcony overhang, so sightlines stay open to the top of the proscenium even at the back — a November 2025 AVFMS reviewer confirmed you are 'pretty high up but atleast you have a full view of the stage'; the tradeoff is distance plus the tight 1920s row spacing the reno preserved.

The Palace's mezz-level boxes are routinely sold as obstructed-view and nytix explicitly warns 'the box seats are not recommended, as they do not provide a clear view of the stage' — the severe side angle means upstage-left blocking is cut off; pick them only if you want the close-in vibe over actually seeing the full stage picture, and never for a dance-heavy or spectacle title.

The balcony survived the lift essentially unchanged — nytix flags that 'the view from the first row of the balcony may be blocked by a large horizontal bar, so sitting in the rows behind the first row is recommended,' and post-reno reviewers still call the balcony 'pretty far' from stage; there is no step-free access, so even the cheapest seat carries real friction.
